content_voiceover: This is the classic exam vignette for acquired methemoglobinemia: cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, usually drug-induced, oxidizes heme iron to the ferric, Fe3+ state, which can't bind oxygen properly. Clinically you get pseudocyanosis with brownish or slate-colored skin and mucosa, but the patient often looks well otherwise. The diagnostic hallmark is the mismatch between a low SaO2 on pulse oximetry and an inappropriately normal or high PaO2 on arterial blood gas, confirmed with a co-oximeter, and the pathognomonic chocolate-brown colored blood that doesn't turn red on exposure to air, unlike normal deoxygenated blood. For causal drugs, memorize the big offenders: local anesthetics like benzocaine, lidocaine, procaine, and prilocaine, plus dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, sulfonamides, acetaminophen or phenacetin, chloroquine, and nitroglycerin. Treatment starts with stopping the offending agent. Give methylene blue at 1 to 2 mg per kg, up to a max of 7 mg per kg, over about 3 to 5 minutes, reserved for patients over 40% methemoglobin or who are symptomatic. Methylene blue works by accelerating the NADPH-dependent pathway to reduce Fe3+ back to Fe2+. Also know that methylene blue is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it can trigger hemolysis, in which case vitamin C or riboflavin are the backup options.
keypoints: Fe3+ (ferric) heme from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency
Diagnostic clue: ↓SaO2 (pulse ox) but normal/high PaO2 (ABG)
Pathognomonic: chocolate-brown blood, doesn't redden with air
Causal drugs: benzocaine, dapsone, primaquine, sulfonamides
Tx: methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg if >40% MHb; avoid in G6PD deficiency
keypoint_voiceover: High-yield points: acquired methemoglobinemia comes from ferric heme iron due to cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency. The classic diagnostic clue is a low pulse oximeter reading with a normal or high PaO2 on blood gas, plus pathognomonic chocolate-brown blood. Watch for causal drugs like benzocaine, dapsone, and primaquine. Treatment is methylene blue for methemoglobin over 40 percent or symptomatic patients, but avoid it in G6PD deficiency, where vitamin C or riboflavin are used instead.
